name: Physical Safety and Security
title: Physical Safety and Security
answer: Physical safety and security in schools covers visitor screening, emergency preparedness and cybersecurity. AI supports these areas by checking visitor identification, drafting realistic drill scenarios and spotting problems in drill reports, and by sending simulated phishing emails to train staff. The decisions that matter, such as denying entry or changing safety procedures, stay with trained staff and the safety team.

sections.body: This idea describes how schools protect people and data across three connected areas: who enters the building, how staff respond in a crisis, and how sensitive information is kept safe from attackers. Visitor management systems screen people at the door by checking identification and sometimes comparing visitors against lists. Emergency drills and tabletop exercises prepare staff to respond to crises, and AI can help draft realistic scenarios and organize drill reports. Cybersecurity matters because schools hold data that attackers want, and phishing is a common way in. The problem this solves is that safety work is broad and easy to let slip, so AI takes on the drafting, organizing and simulating tasks while people keep the judgment calls.
sections.heading: The idea

sections.body: In day to day school life, visitor management systems check identification at the entrance and may compare visitors against lists, with trained staff deciding whether to deny entry. For emergency preparedness, AI can draft realistic scenarios for tabletop exercises, where staff talk through how they would respond, and it can help organize drill reports and flag problems such as a door that takes too long to lock. The safety team then reviews the findings and makes changes. For cybersecurity, training tools such as Microsoft Attack Simulation Training can send simulated phishing emails to staff and teach them to recognize real ones. The text does not give separate grade band guidance for this idea.
sections.heading: How it works in school

sections.body: The text gives no evidence label, study or figure for this idea. It describes practice, such as visitor management systems that check identification, AI drafting tabletop scenarios, AI organizing drill reports, and tools like Microsoft Attack Simulation Training sending simulated phishing emails. This idea therefore rests on practice rather than research as stated in the supplied text.
sections.heading: What the evidence says

sections.body: The text sets clear limits on where AI stops and people decide. Decisions that visitor systems support, such as denying entry, should be made by trained staff, because false matches can embarrass or wrongly exclude parents and visitors. The safety team, not the AI, reviews drill findings and makes changes. Staff who learn to spot a phishing attempt protect every student's data, which places the final judgment with the person reading the message. Nothing here is legal advice, and these are described as practices rather than rules.
